In this lesson, we will explore the rules governing series and parallel circuits, learn how to calculate total resistance, and work through a variety of circuit problems including combined (series-parallel) circuits.

| Property | Series | Parallel |
|---|---|---|
| Current | Same through all components: $I = I_1 = I_2$ | Shared: $I = I_1 + I_2$ |
| Voltage | Shared: $V = V_1 + V_2$ | Same across all branches: $V = V_1 = V_2$ |
| Resistance | Adds up: $R = R_1 + R_2$ | Reciprocals add: $1/R = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2$ |
| Adding more components | Increases total $R$, decreases $I$ | Decreases total $R$, increases $I$ |

: Each device can be switched on or off independently without affecting the others. In a series circuit, if one device is switched off or fails, the circuit is broken and all devices stop working.

: Each device receives the full supply voltage (e.g., 230 V from the mains), regardless of how many other devices are connected. In a series circuit, the voltage would be shared, and each device would receive less than the full voltage.
: Devices can be added or removed without affecting the operation of other devices.
: The other components continue to work. In a series circuit (like old-style Christmas tree lights), if one bulb burns out, the entire string goes dark.
Components need to share the same current (e.g., LEDs in a string that need equal brightness).
A switch is needed to control the entire circuit (switches are in series with the components they control).
Fuses and circuit breakers are placed in series with the circuit they protect.
